newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Venezuelan bolivar volatility seen as a plus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Venezuelan bolivar volatility seen as a plus.

text.p: While the Venezuelan bolivar has been as flat as a pond since exchange controls were removed last April, its recent volatility, although unusual, is only a squall -- and may even be deliberate and welcome, analysts said.
"The Central Bank's trying to re-introduce a correct amount of risk to the foreign exchange and interest rate markets," said Caracas-based Santander analyst Jose Corral.
"I think the change is positive."
Analysts believe the bolivar's volatility may be a Central Bank attempt to discourage short-term capital inflows -- a vexing problem for many emerging markets and particularly Venezuela.

A dose of exchange rate volatility, they say, might reduce the attractiveness to dollar-based investors of high-yielding Central Bank paper, called TEMs -- issued to soak up excess liquidity in Venezuelan financial markets and quell inflationary pressure.
The problem has been investors like TEMs -- too much.

But while that has reduced speculative dollar inflows, it has also kept interest rates in negative territory and imperiled the strong bolivar -- two cornerstones in the central battle against inflation, which has trended downwards from a 15.6 percent peak in May to 2.3 percent in February.
"It was a vicious circle," said Corral. "One consequence of the bolivar's volatility is that it (the circle) may be broken."

On Monday, the bolivar opened at 481 per dollar, leapt in early trade to 491, then plummeted to 474 before finally closing at 480 -- relatively small percentage changes, but also uncharacteristically wild gyrations that left foreign exchange traders worried and confused.

"Those (movements) don't offer any kind of danger to us," Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar reassured Venezuelans in a Tuesday radio interview, although he acknowledged the swings had surprised and worried those more used to exchange rate stability.
That surprise has launched a flurry of front page newspaper articles and worried editorial comment.

But analysts said it was unlikely the bolivar's movements, and nearly two percent depreciation since February 19, were an attempt to cover extra government spending due to a recent 50 percent plus public sector wage increase.

"That would be unlikely. For one, while the wage deal has been done, no-one has been paid yet," said New York based IDEA analyst Gene Freida. State oil company Petroleos de Venezuela remits around $350 million weekly from oil sales so devaluations increase bolivar denominated revenues.

Senior government sources also told Reuters: "The government has absolutely not asked the Central Bank to devalue for fiscal reasons... it looks as though the Bank wants traders to live in a more volatile environment."

And Central Bank president Antonio Casas Gonzalez weighed into the newspaper headline-grabbing debate Monday when he declared: "I want to be emphatic that the Bank's foreign exchange system continues unchanged."
"The system remains the same, namely: a central parity that began at 472 (on January 2), depreciating at 1.32 percent a month with bands 7.5 percent either side," he said in a faxed statement.
For many analysts, the central issue now is interest rates, as it is for Finance Minister Matos.

On Tuesday, Matos extended Venezuela's long-time squabbles with neighboring Colombia to the money markets when he said the bolivar had fallen recently after speculative capital -- most of it Colombian -- had fled Venezuela's low interest rates.
"Rates are so low at present, even Venezuelans don't have anywhere to put savings, except perhaps dollars," said Freida.
"Let's see if TEM rates bounce back on Wednesday," he added.

The Central Bank is to auction 100 billion bolivars ($210 million) at its regular Wednesday auction, with market straw- polls seeing over a one percentage point rise to 14 percent plus in yields on six month paper.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
